title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine but Still Has the Strength to Open a New Front Against NATO
dek: Russian forces have not won in Ukraine, but the war of attrition has produced the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience; the guest argues that Russia is fully capable of launching a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.
why: The guest is the chief foreign correspondent of the Wall Street Journal, who was in Kyiv on the day of the 2022 invasion; his assessment of Russian capabilities and European fractures is far more concrete than that of TV commentators.
who: For those following Eastern European geopolitics, energy, and defense security, as well as foreign-policy readers trying to gauge the real bargaining chips in Russia-Ukraine negotiations.

points.h: Trump's Abandonment Rhetoric, Putin May Take It Seriously
points.body: Everyone is speculating whether John Ratcliffe's secret visit to Russia was about negotiating terms. The guest's judgment is that the visit was more like relaying a message from Trump to Russia: don't take the TV remarks that "America doesn't care about Europe" literally—if Russia invades Lithuania, Estonia, or Finland, the U.S. will send troops. The reasoning is that Moscow is bogged down in a war of attrition in Ukraine and urgently needs to cut off European support for Kyiv; escalating to probe NATO is one option, and Trump's earlier statements like "Europe is a bunch of freeloaders" give Putin room for misreading, hence the need for a dedicated trip to spell out the red lines. To be clear: the guest does not have intelligence from that room; he is explaining why this account "makes complete sense," not confirming it.

points.h: Russian Military Not Exhausted, Can Still Open a Limited Front
points.body: Is Russia, having failed to take Ukraine by force, incapable of opening another front? The guest's answer is direct: it absolutely can fight a "limited front"—not tanks crossing Poland all the way to Paris, but making trouble in the Baltic direction, such as sealing the Suwalki Gap, that narrow land corridor. He says the Russian and Ukrainian armies are the only two forces in the world that have turned modern drone-infantry warfare into a daily routine. Stories of Ukrainian 20-person drone squads wiping out entire traditional battalions are widely told, but the Russian side has the same technology: 20 Russians could equally eliminate a NATO battalion that hasn't been trained against drones. The outside world thinks Russia is getting weaker as the war drags on, but it overlooks that Russia is also the side being tempered in this technological revolution.

points.h: NATO Might Not Even Save Lithuania, Poland Included
points.body: A war game simulating a Russian invasion of Lithuania led the guest to a very unsettling conclusion: even Poland did not send troops to save Lithuania, let alone other allies. The reason is not insufficient military strength, but that Russian forces advance too quickly, and with the shadow of nuclear deterrence, allies would hesitate over "whether to enter," creating a chain of inaction. The guest says Moscow has factored this into its options. He also reminds that this is different from before 2022—then, one could clearly see over a hundred thousand Russian troops massing on the German-Belarusian border; now there is no such physical preparation. Therefore, the most direct escalation may not be a conventional invasion, but more small, ambiguous, deniable attacks (first hitting warehouses or drones).

points.h: Russia Probes NATO's Limits with Drones
points.body: In the current phase without signs of a massed army, Russia still holds a set of low-cost, low-attribution options: launching a limited strike on a NATO warehouse near Poland or Romania, or using captured and modified Ukrainian drones to create incidents, then watching whether NATO splits and whether the U.S. steps in. The guest points out that such probing is already underway—an armed drone struck a Ukrainian aircraft parked at Leipzig Airport in Germany, and only a drone malfunction prevented casualties; Russia's risk-taking behavior is steadily rising, and the West has yet to give a serious response. The senior European officers he has spoken with all believe the most dangerous window is the next one to two years, roughly falling in the final phase of Trump's term—the Kremlin will want to act before the U.S. might let go.

points.h: Putin Wants Ukraine Disarmed, Not a Ceasefire
points.body: Would Putin accept a decent ceasefire agreement? The guest's view is that just looking at what is on the negotiating table makes it clear: Russia's demands have always included not just territory, but also setting a cap on the size of Ukraine's military, restricting the types of weapons, and cutting off Western military aid to Ukraine. In his words, it is to make Ukraine "lose its ability to defend itself"; not neutrality, but "castration," so that it cannot resist again in the next phase of war—a year, five years, or ten years later. Putin signed Minsk-1 and Minsk-2, and violated both. So the guest quotes a former Ukrainian foreign minister's summary: this war will end in only one of two outcomes—the end of Ukraine, or the end of the Russian imperial project. Waiting for the other side to change its mind is not an option.

points.h: Street Protests Can Decide the Fate of a Wartime Cabinet
points.body: Kyiv's recent personnel earthquake appears on the surface to be an anti-corruption storm, but the key mechanism lies elsewhere: wartime has frozen elections, and the president's legitimacy now rests on only one ballast stone—"street support." Zelensky initially fired Defense Minister Fedorov, who championed drone innovation, because he needed the support of Commander-in-Chief Syrskyi; after Fedorov was dismissed, Kyiv's elite took to the streets in protest, small in scale but enough to make the president reverse course—he removed Syrskyi, replaced him with a younger general more popular at the front, and appointed a defense minister with an intelligence background acceptable to all sides. Ukraine's independent anti-corruption agency can still investigate people in the president's innermost circle; Zelensky once tried to amend the law to bring the agency under his control, but within a week he backed down under street pressure. When elections are absent, the square becomes the election.

points.h: Resistance Comes from Memory, Not Heroism
points.body: To sum up Ukrainians' perseverance as patriotic heroism misses what truly drives them. The guest says that after Russian forces take a Ukrainian town, one of the first things they often do is use bulldozers to demolish monuments to the victims of the 1930s Holodomor—they want to erase a memory. Russian state television talks about how to "re-educate" Ukrainians, making them forget their language and culture and become Russians. Around World War II, the Soviet Union carried out systematic purges of Ukraine's cultural elite; the guest, as a child, never knew those writers existed because the collective memory had been wiped out. Today's Ukrainians are almost all descendants of survivors of that meat-grinder history, carrying trauma in their bodies; it is the fear of "never again" that makes them prefer to die on the battlefield than return to those days.

points.h: Half a Million Veterans Held the First Wave of Collapse
points.body: On the night of February 23, 2022, most Kyivites still did not believe there would be war; the guest remembers that his experience in Kabul and Baghdad taught him that "impossible" can flip overnight, but ordinary Ukrainians had no such reference. What truly kept the country from collapsing in the first days was the eight-year war in Donbas: that fighting was far from Kyiv, but it trained roughly 500,000 Ukrainians who had fought against Russian forces, and volunteer organizations evolved into a flexible, daring force. The psychological threshold had already been crossed in Donbas—"we know what they look like, we know how to fight." Because of this experience, Putin's expected quick collapse did not happen, and the West's expectations were also broadly wrong.
